name: Simoom-Basin
description: Simoom-Basin is a world of red-orange dust under the light of two suns. By day, the basin floors shimmer at near-boiling temperatures and dust seas roll in slow, continent-wide tides; by night, the same sands freeze hard enough to crack. A canyon system deeper than any on record bisects the southern hemisphere, its walls striped with the mineral ghosts of a vanished sea.

There is almost no sound here—only wind, thin and whistling, moving grit along the canyon rims with a sound like dry breathing. The double sunset paints everything copper and then violet within minutes, and the temperature falls so fast that frost forms on stone before full dark. Travelers describe an enormous, patient silence that makes voices feel intrusive.

The dead riverbeds were a puzzle for decades: they branch like drainage networks but no water has flowed on Simoom-Basin in geological ages. The answer lives in them still—endolithic microbial crusts, black-green films tucked beneath translucent pebbles, drawing moisture from the atmosphere itself each dawn. The crusts follow the ancient river courses precisely, as if remembering water their ancestors once drank.

Survey teams come for the silicon and iron, but the biologists stay for the crusts, which photosynthesize using both suns simultaneously and repair radiation damage faster than any known organism. Every sample shipped out has died within hours, which means the only living archive of this biochemistry is the planet itself. Mining charters are already being written for the riverbeds, and no law yet exists to stop the bulldozers.
